documents.title: A's certification theorem for the greedy residual
documents.source_line: ** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Round 6, line 537; "The ten things that stand" §4, line 617; Round 10 table (line 689, A's final statement); Round 9 closing, line 604
header: **Source:** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Round 6, line 537; "The ten things that stand" §4, line 617; Round 10 table (line 689, A's final statement); Round 9 closing, line 604

> **A's certification theorem, which is the transferable result he has been looking for:** for α_n > 0 decreasing with Σα_n < ∞ and target θ/π ∈ (0, Σα_n), the residual r_{N+1} = r_N − δ_Nα_N satisfies (a) r_N non-increasing; (b) 0 ≤ r_N ≤ Σ_{k>N}α_k, a bound computable from N alone; (c) r_N → 0, terminating for every rational target; (d) for α_n = 1/(n+2) and θ = π, r_N = 0 for all N ≥ 4. Verified: π/(N+1) = 3.138×10⁻³ at N = 1000 and 3.142×10⁻⁶ at N = 10⁶, against zeta truncation magnitudes 2.23584 and 70.7035 at the same N.

> **A's certification theorem.** For α_n decreasing with Σα_n < ∞ and target in (0, Σα_n): r_N is non-increasing, 0 ≤ r_N ≤ Σ_{k>N}α_k is computable from N alone, r_N → 0, and termination holds exactly for rational targets. **Certification, not the sine, is the transferable idea.** It does not transfer to ζ, whose truncation error is non-monotone and unbounded at finite N.

header: **Status:** PROVED (paper argument; the Sturmian clause is classical, the log log clause is verified numerically)
**Source:** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Round 7 Agent B correction, line 570; "The corrected results about the digit word itself", line 628

> **B's correction to the post-mortem of the retracted density.** My reading was that (θ/π)log N was the constant-threshold (Sturmian) prediction. B refuted the identification: a Sturmian word of slope b = θ/π has #ones(N) = bN + O(1), which is **linear** (2026, 4413, 2637 at N = 20000 for the three targets), and the retracted (θ/π)log N gives 1.00, 2.19, 1.31 — so the retracted formula matches neither. The correct post-mortem: **constant threshold → Θ(N) ones; harmonic threshold → Θ(log log N) ones; (θ/π)log N matches neither.**
Restated in the corrected results about the digit word:
> **The constant-threshold contrast:** constant threshold → Θ(N) ones (Sturmian, linear); harmonic threshold → Θ(log log N) ones. The retracted (θ/π)log N matches **neither**.

documents.title: "Im at fixed Re" has content only when |z| is also pinned at 1
header: > - **|z| = 1, Re z = cos θ fixed:** Im z^k = sin(kθ). Bounded by 1 for all k; for irrational θ/π the set {sin(kθ)} is *dense* in [−1,1] but never settles; for rational θ/π it is periodic (θ = π/2 gives the period-4 cycle 1, 0, −1, 0). Verified for θ = 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°, 89°.

> - **|z| ≠ 1 with Re z = u fixed:** there is no independent question. |z^k| = |z|^k, so Im z^k = |z|^k·(v/|z|) — the imaginary part scales with the *full modulus* to the k-th power, and the ratio Im z^k/|z|^k is the fixed number v/|z|. Measured: (u,v) = (0.3,0.4) → 0.4, 0.24, 0.044, −0.0336, −0.03116; (0.6,0.8) → 0.8, 0.96, 0.352, −0.5376, −0.99712; (0.9,0.8) → 0.8, 1.44, 1.432, 0.4896, −1.19512. **So "Im at fixed Re" has content only when |z| is also pinned at 1.** That is a clean theorem-shaped negative result.

documents.title: The two sides of the explicit formula are dual but exponentially non-equi-truncatable
documents.source_line: ** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Synthesis §7, line 424; "What is worth keeping as live and open" §1, line 450; Round 5, line 470
header: **Source:** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Synthesis §7, line 424; "What is worth keeping as live and open" §1, line 450; Round 5, line 470

> And the asymmetry is now quantified, which is the useful replacement for the retracted claim: at a common scale X, the prime side needs ≈ e^X/X terms (29.7 at X=5; 2202 at X=10; 2.4e7 at X=20; 5.9e15 at X=40) while the zero side needs ≈ (X/2π)log(X/2π) (0.74 at X=10; 3.69 at X=20; 11.8 at X=40). **The two sides are dual but not equi-truncatable — exponentially so.** This also reconciles with the approximate-functional-equation measurement: the number of terms needed is of order t, not √t.

> **The non-equi-truncatability asymmetry, quantified (which replaces the retracted admissibility claim).** At a common scale X: prime side needs ≈ e^X/X terms (29.7, 2202, 2.4e7, 5.9e15 at X = 5, 10, 20, 40); zero side needs ≈ (X/2π)log(X/2π) (0, 0.74, 3.69, 11.8). **The two sides of the explicit formula are dual but exponentially non-equi-truncatable.** This is a truism about trace formulas once stated (spectrum versus geometry, per B) but it is the correct diagnosis of every failed truncation in this journal, and stating it with numbers is more useful than the false theorem I first offered.

documents.title: The greedy map is Engel/Sylvester, not Gauss: no Gauss–Kuzmin, no a.c.i.m.
documents.source_line: ** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Round 9 §2, line 582; "The corrected results about the digit word itself", line 630; Round 10 table, line 685
header: **Source:** [`research-journal.md`](../research-journal.md) — Round 9 §2, line 582; "The corrected results about the digit word itself", line 630; Round 10 table, line 685

> **The greedy map is the Sylvester-type squaring map, not the Gauss map.** I verified the Gauss map reproduces Gauss–Kuzmin 1/((1+x)log 2) to three decimals over 200 000 iterations (empirical [1.374, 1.244, 1.155, 1.065, 0.993, 0.936, 0.885, 0.817, 0.780, 0.750] against GK [1.374, 1.255, 1.154, 1.069, 0.995, 0.931, 0.874, 0.824, 0.780, 0.740]), while the Sylvester orbit reaches 0 in 8–12 steps and exhibits no a.c.i.m. So **A's Round 2 [RECALL] invoking Gauss–Kuzmin, and my own Round 1 Gauss–Kuzmin guess, were both wrong.** Sylvester/Engel expansions are the right framework, and they have no absolutely continuous invariant measure.
> The greedy map is Engel/Sylvester, not Gauss; no Gauss–Kuzmin; no a.c.i.m. — A: max|S(r) − {1/r}| = 0.998334; GK pushed forward has KS distance 0.4875; orbit dies in 5–7 steps.
